data.title: Seborrhoeic dermatitis — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Seborrhoeic dermatitis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define seborrhoeic dermatitis.**
- Chronic relapsing inflammatory dermatosis in sebum-rich areas (scalp, face, chest, flexures), characterised by red patches with greasy yellowish scales; dandruff (pityriasis capitis) is its mildest form

**Q2. Who gets it? (bimodal)**
- Infants (first 3 months — cradle cap, napkin/flexures; self-limiting) and adults (30–60 years, men more)
- Higher prevalence and severity in HIV (30–80%), Parkinson's disease and other neurological disorders (facial immobility, sebum pooling), Down syndrome, depression, alcoholism, after neuroleptics

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Malassezia yeasts (M. globosa, M. restricta) metabolise sebum triglycerides into irritant free fatty acids (oleic acid) → inflammation in susceptible individuals (barrier defects)
- Sebum quantity is not necessarily increased; host immune response, stress, cold dry weather contribute

**Q4. Clinical features in adults.**
- Scalp: diffuse fine scaling to thick adherent greasy scales with erythema, may extend to forehead hairline (corona seborrhoica)
- Face: eyebrows, glabella, nasolabial folds, beard, eyelids (blepharitis), ears (retroauricular fissuring, external canal)
- Trunk: petaloid (annular) lesions on presternal/interscapular areas, pityriasiform type
- Flexures: axillae, groin, submammary, umbilicus — intertrigo-like
- Seborrhoeic erythroderma (rare)

**Q5. Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis vs infantile atopic dermatitis.**
- Seborrhoeic: onset first weeks, greasy yellow scales, scalp/flexures/napkin area involved, little itch, baby comfortable, resolves by 6–12 months
- Atopic: onset after 2–3 months, cheeks/extensors, napkin area spared, very itchy, irritable baby, family history, chronic course

**Q6. What is Leiner's disease?**
- Historical term — generalised seborrhoeic-like erythroderma in infants with diarrhoea, failure to thrive and recurrent infections; now linked to immunodeficiency (C3/C5 dysfunction, SCID, Omenn)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Scalp: psoriasis (sharply defined, silvery scale, beyond hairline, nails), tinea capitis, atopic dermatitis, pityriasis amiantacea, LCH (infants), head lice
- Face: rosacea, lupus (malar), contact dermatitis, tinea faciei, perioral dermatitis
- Trunk: pityriasis versicolor, pityriasis rosea, secondary syphilis, Darier's disease
- 'Sebopsoriasis' — overlap

**Q8. Why test for HIV in severe seborrhoeic dermatitis?**
- Sudden onset, extensive, severe or treatment-resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis in a young adult may be an early marker of HIV infection

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Scalp: antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole 2%, ciclopirox 1%, selenium sulphide 2.5%, zinc pyrithione) 2–3 times weekly with 5 min contact; keratolytics (salicylic acid, coal tar) for thick scales; short course of steroid lotion/ foam (betamethasone, clobetasol shampoo)
- Face/body: ketoconazole 2% cream, mild steroid (hydrocortisone/desonide) for short periods, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus) as steroid-sparing, roflumilast 0.3% foam (newer topical PDE4 inhibitor)
- Blepharitis: lid hygiene with dilute baby shampoo
- Infants: emollient/olive oil to soften crusts, gentle brushing, mild shampoo; ketoconazole cream if needed
- Severe/extensive: oral itraconazole 200 mg/day for 7 days then 2 days/month maintenance, fluconazole; isotretinoin low dose; phototherapy NB-UVB
- Maintenance shampoo once weekly to prevent relapse

**Q10. Histopathology.**
- Psoriasiform and spongiotic dermatitis with parakeratosis around follicular ostia ('shoulder parakeratosis'), neutrophils in scale crusts; yeasts in scale

**Q11. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q12. Dermoscopy of scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis vs psoriasis.**
- Seborrhoeic: yellowish greasy scales, arborising thin red lines and atypical vessels, structureless red areas, honeycomb pigment
- Psoriasis: silvery-white scales, regularly distributed red dots/ globules and twisted red loops

**Q13. Seborrhoeic dermatitis in neurological disease — why?**
- Parkinson's disease (increased sebum, facial immobility, autonomic dysfunction), post-stroke, spinal cord injury, facial nerve palsy (on affected side), syringomyelia — sebum pooling and Malassezia proliferation

**Q14. Drugs that induce seborrhoeic dermatitis-like eruptions.**
- Neuroleptics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine), lithium, buspirone, methyldopa, cimetidine, interferon, gold, psoralens, EGFR/ BRAF inhibitors, dupilumab (head-neck dermatitis)

**Q15. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q16. Seborrhoeic blepharitis — management.**
- Scaling of eyelid margins with crusts and redness; warm compresses, lid scrubs with diluted baby shampoo/ commercial lid cleansers twice daily, topical ketoconazole cream cautiously on eyelid skin, artificial tears; ophthalmology referral if keratitis

## Quick spotter facts
- Greasy yellow scales on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds — seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Severe sudden seb derm in young adult — test HIV; also Parkinson's

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Seborrhoeic dermatitis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
